approachQuestion.prompt:
First uninterrupted download slot

A download needs d uninterrupted time units on a link. Unsorted half-open outage intervals [start,end) may overlap or nest. Find the earliest integer start t ≥ T for which [t,t+d) intersects no outage, or return −1 if it cannot finish by H. Outages may extend outside [T,H). Do not modify the input.

Input: T=0, H=15, d=4, outages=[[7,9],[1,3],[2,5]]
Output: 9
The gap [5,7) is too short; [9,13) is the first feasible download.

Input: T=3, H=9, d=3, outages=[[6,8]]
Output: 3
Ending exactly when an outage begins is permitted.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ T < H ≤ 1000000000; 1 ≤ d ≤ H−T; 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1000000000. Use comparison ordering. Return only t.

options.text: Sort copied outages by start and set candidate=T. Before processing each outage, return −1 if candidate+d exceeds H. Skip outages ending at or before candidate. If candidate+d is at most the next outage start, return candidate. Otherwise move candidate to that outage’s end. After the scan, return candidate if candidate+d ≤ H, else −1.
options.feedback: A conflicting outage rules out the current start and every later start before its end. Moving to its end is the earliest remaining possibility; ordered processing prevents overlooking an earlier usable gap.

options.text: Merge the outages and return the start of the longest free gap in [T,H), provided its length is at least d.
options.feedback: The longest gap need not be earliest. For T=0,H=20,d=2,outages=[[3,10]], the earliest start is 0, not 10 at the longest gap.

options.text: Use the candidate-frontier scan, but accept a gap only when candidate+d is strictly less than the next outage start.
options.feedback: For T=3,H=9,d=3,outages=[[6,8]], [3,6) is feasible. Requiring strict inequality misses the earliest start 3.

options.text: Try each integer t from T through H−d and scan all outages to test [t,t+d), returning the first feasible t.
options.feedback: Integer endpoints guarantee an integer earliest answer, so the search is correct. But it enumerates the potentially huge time domain and repeatedly scans outages instead of jumping across conflicts.

feedback.reason: Find the earliest gap of sufficient length by jumping a candidate past conflicts, preserving half-open contact.
details: Copy outages, sort by start with iterative bottom-up merge sort and one buffer, and scan once with a candidate start. Before each outage, fail if candidate+d exceeds H; skip outages ending at or before candidate. Accept candidate when it finishes at or before the next start. Otherwise move it to the conflicting outage’s end. After the scan, apply the horizon check again. Do not build a merged list or inspect individual time units.

A candidate ending exactly at the next half-open outage's start fits. On conflict, move to the outage end and continue; overlapping outages may push it farther. Recheck the horizon after the final outage.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For candidate-frontier, n is the outage count. Include input copy and sort buffer. Choose the tightest standard worst-case pair.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)

feedback.reason: Sort outages and examine each once, independent of horizon magnitude.
details: Sorting costs O(n log n); each outage is then examined at most once. The copy and reusable buffer take O(n), with constant iterative scan state. The size of the time horizon does not multiply the running time.
Iterative comparison merge sort; constant-time sums with no overflow.
“Time O(Hn), auxiliary space O(1)”: The method jumps directly to interval ends and never enumerates H time units; it also allocates copied outages and a sorting buffer.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The scan is linear only after the copy is comparison-sorted; the sorting cost remains part of the method.
“Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)”: The copied outages and merge buffer use linear auxiliary space despite the scalar answer.
